title: The trust problem — why Bitcoin's breakthrough is bigger than most understand
tweets:
The entire history of money is a history of trust.

Trust in the king not to debase the coin. Trust in the bank not to gamble the deposit. Trust in the government not to inflate the savings away.

Every system required you to trust someone. Until Bitcoin. 🧵

Trust has a cost most people never account for.

When you trust an institution with your money, you give them the ability to say no.

No to your withdrawal. No to your transaction. No to your account. The trust relationship is never symmetrical — they hold the leverage.

Governments have frozen accounts. Banks have failed. Payment processors have deplatformed.

These aren't anomalies. They're features of systems built on permission.

If someone can grant you access, someone can revoke it.

Bitcoin replaced the trusted party with a protocol.

The rules are public, enforced by mathematics, and cannot be changed by any single actor.

The network doesn't have an agenda. It doesn't know who you are. It doesn't care what your government thinks of you.

This is the actual breakthrough.

Not "number go up." Not a new investment asset.

The first time in history that a monetary system's rules are enforced by math rather than by men — and every individual can verify them independently.

This isn't anti-bank ideology. It's engineering.

Bitcoin doesn't ask you to trust it. It asks you to verify it.

That's a different category of system — and understanding why changes how you see every institution that came before it.
